entries.title: UK: Man charged over suspected role in Rwanda genocide
entries.summary: The suspect has been accused of directing and inciting acts of murder and genocide carried out by others in Rwanda.
entries.content:
September 21, 2026

The suspect has been accused of directing and inciting acts of murder and genocide carried out by others in Rwanda.

UK authorities arrested and charged a man on Monday over alleged links to the Rwandan genocide, prosecutors and the London police said. It was the first arrest of its kind, although authorities have been pursuing the case for several years.

The 65-year-old man has been charged with one count of being an ancillary to genocide and six offenses of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, officials said.

"This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes," said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counterterror policing.

The Rwandan genocide took place in 1994, where over 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate ethnic Hutus ⁠were killed in a 100-day rampage, orchestrated and led by the Hutu ruling majority. Local officials and ordinary citizens were involved in the mass killing.

UK law allows prosecutors to bring charges for some international offenses, including genocide and crimes against humanity, even if the crimes were committed abroad.

It is the latest case of an arrest in Europe of someone linked to Rwanda's genocide. In July, a German-Rwandan national was arrested for charges of taking part in the genocide and killing one person himself.

Meanwhile, in the Netherlands, a man was sentenced to life in prison for having taken part in attacks on homes, including launching a grenade on sheltering Tutsi civilians.

Suspect underwent name change

UK's Metropolitan Police war crimes investigators opened the case against the suspect in 2019, following a request by the Rwandan government.

The 65-year-old is originally from Kigali but lived in London at the time of the arrest.

He reportedly entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998, according to Rwandan Justice Minister Tharcisse Karugarama.

After being granted British citizenship in 2004, the man underwent a name change, and two years later, he was arrested over his connection to the genocide.

His extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was ultimately halted by a British UK court in 2017.

The failed extradition prompted the Rwandan government to urge UK authorities to investigate the matter themselves.

Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's counterterror division, said the man is "alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others."

Authorities say investigations are ongoing for more suspects who are linked to the Rwandan genocide currently living in Britain.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: US-China rivalry is reshaping global trade — and Europe is caught in the middle.
entries.summary: China's Xi Jinping is traveling to Washington this week. Regardless of what comes from his talks with US President Trump, the EU will likely remain stuck between erratic US trade policy and Beijing's export machine.
entries.content:
North America

As US and China talk, middle powers jostle for position

September 21, 2026

China's Xi Jinping is traveling to Washington this week. Regardless of what comes from his talks with US President Trump, the EU will likely remain stuck between erratic US trade policy and Beijing's export machine.

Last week, German and Chinese business leaders met in the German city of Düsseldorf for an economic dialogue. Although the panel focused on trade, and investment between China and Europe, ongoing US-China rivalry was the elephant in the room.

As Xi Jinping and Donald Trump sit down in the US capital Washington this week, there is some hope that talks will show progress on alleviating the ongoing trade war launched by the US president. The last time the two leaders met at a Beijing summit in May did not yield any tangible results.

"The assumption in Beijing, and that's the way they're operating, is that China and the US will hold each other in check for the foreseeable future," Mikko Huotari, director of the Berlin-based China think tank MERICS, told a policy briefing last week.

"Xi really doesn't need a breakthrough in Washington. He needs more time. And the same is true for Washington. So we have this strategic stalemate situation, which I think is the best description of what we see currently."

A deal could benefit Trump's Republican Party ahead of the important US midterm elections in November, but that outcome remains far from certain.

"We will discuss everything,"Trump said about Xi's visit to the White House.

Cooperation on AI?

Beijing and Washington are competing on multiple levels, and nowhere is this rivalry more consequential than with artificial intelligence (AI).

The US government prohibits the export of high-performance chips to China. Beijing, in turn, restricts the export of rare earth elements, which are indispensable for semiconductor production.

And amid concerns about the dangers of unregulated AI, there is some expectation that Xi and Trump will discuss AI guardrails during their talks. Xi has called for international cooperation on AI development, while Trump sees its regulation as a threat to the US' leadership in the field. 

After meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that US and Chinese officials have already discussed creating a "notification mechanism" to share information about AI-related security incidents.

Europe's 'China shock'

From a European perspective, both China and the US are currently considered difficult partners.

The second "China shock … is already here" in Europe, said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her 2026 State of the Union address last week.

The first "China shock" came 25 years ago, triggered by China's accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), when inexpensive "Made in China" products began to flood the global markets.

The second one stems from Chinas technological progress in industries such as battery technology, green energy and mobility.

"It shows in our communities and in factories across our Union. It leads to deindustrialization in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable," von der Leyen said in her address.

The EU is aiming for a rapid transition to e-mobility and wants to drastically reduce CO2 emissions from road traffic. At the same time, Brussels is calling for additional tariffs on low-cost electric cars from China, as China enjoys competitive advantages with cheaper cars and high government subsidies.

China denies having an unfair advantage, and German automakers VW and BMW also oppose punitive tariffs due to potential revenue losses resulting from Chinese retaliatory measures.

A Chinese participant at the Düsseldorf economic dialogue told DW anonymously that China's domestic consumption cannot absorb manufacturing.

"China's economy is weak. Companies are worried about their business and urgently need to tap into foreign markets," said the Chinese executive, who used to work in the European branch of a Chinese state-owned enterprise.

Trump pressuring EU over China, but also on trade, security

"Against the backdrop of the ongoing escalation of strategic rivalry between the US and China, the US is constantly urging its allies to tighten restrictions on China in the areas of technology, supply chains, and security," said Yang Xiepu, director of the Center for Sino-German Cooperation at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).

At the same time, Trump frequently threatens the EU with tariffs while injecting instability into the strategic NATO alliance. When the EU offered Canada "associate membership" last week, Trump floated the possibility of new punitive measures from the US.

While  Carney expressed interest , Trump called the idea "ridiculous."

"If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said, without specifying what he considers about EU-Canada ties to be "hostile."

Copying Canada's 'middle' approach

Facing Trump administration's tariff upsets and caustic rhetoric, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is openly hedging his bets on the world stage.

"We know the old order is not coming back. We shouldn't mourn it," he declared at the 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos in January, with the US allies rattled by Trump threatening to annex Greenland from Denmark.

Carney said that great powers can "afford for now to go it alone" but middle powers need to work better together.

"When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what's offered. We compete with each other to be the most accommodating. This is not sovereignty," Carney told the forum.

"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he emphasized.

In early 2026, Carney visited China and agreed to a "new-era strategic partnership." Ottawa subsequently lowered import tariffs on Chinese electric cars from 100% to 6.1%. The quota stands at 49,000 vehicles per year.

Separately, China has launched a charm offensive toward US allies, "more specifically, the fragile allies," according to MERICS Director Mikko Huotari.

For example, Xi attended the BRICS summit in India in September despite the rocky relationship with New Delhi. He also attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan. In November, China will host the G-20 summit.

Carney has described this new form of diplomacy as "variable geometry" — different alliances for different issues based on common values and interests. In November, he will travel to Shenzhen for the APECE summit. He will also be at the table there — and hopefully not on the menu.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: US news outlets sue Trump over White House ban
entries.summary: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico say the ban against them threatens press freedom and the right to independent journalism.
entries.content:
September 21, 2026

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico say the ban against them threatens press freedom and the right to independent journalism.

US news outlets CNN, MS NOW, and Politico plan to go to court against Donald Trump's administration, after he banned them from the White House, the three said in a statement on Monday.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in their statement.

The announcement comes after Trump accused the media outlets of reporting "fiction" and "lied" in their coverage of his administration.

On Monday, Trump wrote on social media that his administration was not targeting "the Free Press" but was "instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer."

Trump's media ban is the latest escalation in his long-running feud with several US media outlets. In 2017, as he began his first presidential term, he blasted the press as "the enemy of the American people."

What did CNN, MS NOW, Politico say?

A day after Trump's announcement, the entry badges of reporters for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico had been disabled.

The news outlets accused the White House of revoking their journalists' credentials "without notice or process" because the administration "objected to our reporting."

"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," they said in the statement.

The banned news outlets argued in their lawsuit that the constitution "does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

White House pool coverage suspended

CNN is one of five news organizations, including broadcasters ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC, that make up the White House television pool. The broadcasters share the costs of covering the president, take turns organizing coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

On Monday, in response to CNN's exclusion from the White House television pool, the other major TV networks said they have suspended their coverage, which effectively eliminates the most important video source for White House events.

CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump's trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly on Monday, but as a result of the ban, it was not able ‌to provide a pool feed.

Bryan Boughton, who runs the Fox News Washington bureau and the current TV pool chair, announced the suspension in an email Monday.

"This follows the White House's position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties," Boughton added. "There will be no replacement pool put in place," he added.

The lack of replacement reflected an effective boycott over the ban.

ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC addressed the situation in a statement, saying that "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Nuclear power is back on Southeast Asia's energy agenda
entries.summary: Rising electricity demand, shocks in energy security and climate commitments are reviving long-stalled plans for nuclear power across Southeast Asia. But proponents of nuclear energy still face major obstacles.
entries.content:
September 21, 2026

Rising electricity demand, shocks in energy security and climate commitments are reviving long-stalled plans for nuclear power across Southeast Asia. But proponents of nuclear energy still face major obstacles.

Southeast Asian governments are revisiting nuclear power as electricity consumption raises, exposing the region's dependence on fossil fuels.

The rise is largely driven by new factories, electric vehicles and the region's rush to host data centers against the backdrop of countries trying to reduce carbon emissions.

No Southeast Asian nation currently operates a commercial nuclear power plant, but several are placing their bets on nuclear energy and reviving plans that had been stalled for years.

On September 8, Vietnam's state-owned Petrovietnam and South Korea's KEPCO agreed to deepen cooperation on the planned Ninh Thuan 2 nuclear plan in Vietnamt. Six days later, Singapore's government said it was studying nuclear power and small modular reactors (SMRs)with an "open mind", though it stressed that it had not made a decision.

Vietnam wants to bring its two Ninh Thuan plants into operation by 2035 and pursue at least one SMR project.

Indonesia plans an initial 500 megawatts of nuclear capacity, with units targeted to begin operating in 2032, while the Philippines is working towards its first 1,200 MW of nuclear capacity from the same year.

Thailand's latest draft power plan proposes its first SMR in 2037, while Malaysia and Singapore remain at the study stage.

Energy shocks vs. the shadow of Fukushima

The renewed interest marks a sharp reversal from the caution that followed Japan's Fukushima nuclear disaster in 2011.

The accident stalled several Southeast Asian countries' plans to pursue nuclear energy, Alvin Chew, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, told DW.

But a string of geopolitical shocks in recent years has changed the energy debate.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) says Southeast Asia's electricity generation has risen by around 60% since 2015. Coal supplied most of that increase, pushing its share of regional generation from 37% to 47%.

The war in Ukraine and the current Middle East crisis have heightened energy-security concerns for developing countries, even as most Southeast Asian governments have committed to net-zero emissions by 2050 or 2060, Chew said.

The region's electricity demand is forecast to grow by an average of 5.3% a year between 2026 and 2030.

"Nuclear energy is deemed to be the viable solution to address both challenges of climate and energy security," Chew said.

Appeal of modular reactors

One reason governments are reconsidering nuclear power is that today's technology is starkly different from what was used 15 years ago in Fukushima.

SMRs have broadened the range of possible projects. Unlike conventional reactors, SMRs are designed as smaller units that can potentially be added in stages.

"In the past, deploying nuclear energy generally meant building very large conventional reactors, involving long construction periods, enormous upfront investments and requiring electricity grids capable of absorbing very large generating units," Jie-Sheng Tan-Soo, assistant professor and director at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy in Singapore, told DW.

"SMRs have changed the nuclear conversation in Southeast Asia because they potentially make nuclear compatible with smaller grids, smaller countries and more incremental investment," he added.

That does not mean SMRs will solve nuclear power's economics. Many designs remain at an early stage of deployment, meaning promises of cheaper construction through mass production have yet to be demonstrated on a broad commercial scale.

Another force pushing nuclear energy back onto the agenda is the rapid expansion of data centers, which require large quantities of reliable electricity, Julius Cesar Trajano, a research fellow with the Centre for Non-Traditional Security Studies at RSIS, told DW.

The IEA expects electricity consumption from Southeast Asian data centers to more than double by 2030.

More than 70% of existing regional data-center capacity is concentrated in Singapore and Johor in southern Malaysia.

"Countries are therefore approaching nuclear energy with greater emphasis on governance and regulatory capacity than during earlier attempts," said Trajano.

Building a nuclear safety net

The hardest problems, however, remain much the same. Nuclear plants, even SMRs, still require a lot of time and money, and newcomer countries must establish independent regulators, train specialist workforces and develop credible systems for radioactive waste and emergency response.

Geography adds another layer of difficulty. Parts of Southeast Asia are vulnerable to earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis, making site selection and emergency planning particularly sensitive.

Nuclear power also places unusually heavy demands on state institutions, Tan-Soo said. Governments need institutions that take a long time to establish and must remain reliable for decades.

"For countries developing nuclear power for the first time, building this ecosystem can take as much effort as building the plant itself," he added.

Long road to wielding nuclear power

Public support is another matter. A Philippine government survey released last year found that more than 70% of respondents supported nuclear energy's potential role in providing electricity.

By contrast, the Indonesia Energy Transition Outlook 2026 reported that 78% of respondents placed nuclear as their least-preferred energy source.

"The biggest obstacle is the political will to proceed with adoption of nuclear energy, which, to a certain extent, is dependent on public perception," said Chew.

Southeast Asia's highly varied national capacities and electricity systems also make a common pathway unlikely, Trajano said.

Vietnam has revived plans for large conventional plants, Indonesia and Thailand are giving greater attention to SMRs, while Singapore is still building the expertise needed to determine whether nuclear power is suitable at all.

"There is clearly much more political momentum behind nuclear power in Southeast Asia today than there was a decade ago, and I think some countries could ultimately deploy it," Tan-Soo said.

"But moving from announcing a nuclear ambition to financing, licensing, constructing and safely operating a reactor is an enormous step."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Why gender-based violence persists in Southern Africa
entries.summary: A series of killings in South Africa has renewed scrutiny of efforts to combat violence against women. Activists say laws alone are not enough without effective implementation.
entries.content:
September 21, 2026

A series of killings in South Africa has renewed scrutiny of efforts to combat violence against women. Activists say laws alone are not enough without effective implementation.

On Thursday, police in South Africa found the pattially naked body of Dineo M. The 38-year-old had been beaten and stabbed to death in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city.

This is one of a series of killings of women in their 20s and 30s in Ekurhuleni over the past two months.

But for Dineo's sister, Carol, this is much more than another statistic in a country where gender-based violence (GBV) was declared a national disaster in 2025.

"We sit here today and we will never see her walk through the door. Her 2-year-old has no idea what is going on," Carol told DW. "How do you explain to her [...] your mother was brutally murdered, dumped behind shrubs, left unrecognizable? [...] That is why you don't have a mother today."

A community on edge

Authorities said it was not yet clear whether the killings were linked. However, they said they have identified similarities, and have issued an alert for women in Ekurhuleni to take precautions.

Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said on Sunday that so far there was no conclusive evidence that the killings were carried out by a serial killer, "but nothing has yet been excluded while investigations continue."

For families and communities, the deaths have raised fresh questions about whether existing measures are enough to protect women.

South African Minister in the Presidency for Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities Sindisiwe Chikunga said at a protest march in Johannesburg that violence against women often starts behind closed doors.

"Please, stop it. Stop raping women. Stop insulting women. Stop financially abusing women," she said, warning that verbal abuse can escalate. "They start with insults. They proceed to assault and then to murder. It cannot be."

Why laws fall short

For Naledi Masipa, campaigns manager at Gender Links, an NGO promoting gender justice across Southern Africa, the problem encompasses all of society.

"Having laws and policies does not automatically change what happens in communities and households," she told DW, adding that the entire support system must work, from reporting and policing to health services, psychosocial support and legal assistance.

If one part fails, she said, women continue to carry the burden. "The real test is whether a woman in an ordinary community feels safer."  

Amnesty International South Africa said the response to the crimes must recognize the gendered nature of killings.

"Femicide itself is not recognized as a crime. It's just seen as another murder," said Tegan Snyman, a research assistant at the international non-governmental organization, pointing out that South Africa had declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis. She argued that more resources were necessary as well as a sense of urgency. 

A regional challenge

The neighboring country of Botswana also struggles with high levels of gender-based violence.

Natasha Rampa, a permanent secretary in Botswana's Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs, said that "at least 37% of women in Botswana have experienced violence in their lifetimes."

In June, Botswana and the United Nations launched a joint program focused on prevention, survivor-centered services and stronger institutions.

"Violence is unacceptable, and we must work together as a society to address this issue," Minister of Youth and Gender Affairs Lesego Chombo told parliament. He said that tackling gender-based violence (GBV) requires action beyond government.

Turning policy into protection

Zambia also faces persistent gender-based violence — despite laws and national programs aimed at tackling it.

Anne Mbewe-Anamela, the executive director of the Non-Governmental Coordinating Council, an umbrella organization in the country that champions gender equality, said the response must put survivors at the center.

"GBV is deeply rooted in power, inequality, and social expectations," she told DW. "We can have strong laws, but if communities still believe violence is a private matter or a normal part of marriage, then survivors remain silent and trapped."

For activists across the region, the challenge is, therefore, not simply creating more policies. It is making protection, support and justice work in practice. And for families like Dineo's, that difference is painfully personal. Carol knows her sister will never walk through the door again.

She wants Dineo's daughter to grow up understanding that what happened to her mother was not normal and that women deserve to be safe.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: India's road rage: When cars become weapons
entries.summary: Road disputes are turning violent across India, raising questions about status and impunity behind the wheel for drivers of expensive cars.
entries.content:
India

India's road rage: When cars become weapons

September 21, 2026

Road disputes are turning violent across India, raising questions about status and impunity behind the wheel for drivers of expensive cars.

A road altercation in Gurugram, a suburb of New Delhi, went viral last week after a 27-year-old female biker was allegedly chased and hit by a car.

The two sides gave differing accounts of the initial dispute, with the car driver telling Indian media that the group of bikers overtook his car and slowed down in front of it.

In turn, the motorcycle rider, Shivani Chauhan, said the car was following her and the argument started when she asked the people inside to keep a safe distance.

Chauhan's motorcycle-mounted camera shows the car hitting her from the side and them speeding away as she falls and rolls on the road.

"I could have suffered serious fractures or internal injuries and even died. Due to such people, the roads of Gurugram and Delhi feel unsafe," Chauhan was quoted as saying by Indian news outlets.

According to reports, the driver claims that he lost control of his vehicle and left the scene because he feared reprisals from the biker group. Police have since arrested the driver on charges including attempted murder and stalking.

Road rage escalates to violence, shootouts

The case was only the latest example of how quickly a dispute on India's increasingly crowded roads can turn violent.

In March in Hassan, in the southern Karnataka state, young men reportedly shouted at the driver of a Toyota Fortuner SUV to slow down.

Police said the driver turned the vehicle around and rammed the group, killing one man and seriously injuring three others.

In the northern city of Dehradun that month, an argument over giving way between two SUVs, a Toyota Fortuner and a Mahindra Scorpio, escalated into a chase and gunfire.

The altercation cost the life of one man, a retired Army brigadier Mukesh Joshi, who was not involved in the initial dispute.

"The occupants of the Scorpio waited outside the club till early morning and then chased the Fortuner. During the firing, the brigadier, who was out on a morning walk, was hit by a bullet in the chest," said senior superintendent of police Pramendra Dobhal.

Concerns over road safety prompted the administration of Daman, a small coastal town north of Mumbai, to take an unusual step. On September 9, officials gathered owners of Mahindra Thar and Toyota Fortuner SUVs and made them take a public road safety pledge.

District Collector Saurabh Mishra, the district's top administrator, warned that these kinds of larger vehicles should not be used to intimidate others or display power.

More cars, less space on Indian roads

India's roads are notoriously dangerous, with government figures showing 485 people were killed in crashes on an average day in 2024. The data also indicates that the number of vehicles is currently growing much faster than the expansion of the road network.

Notably, SUVs accounted for about 2.63 million vehicles, or 56% of India's car sales, in the 12 months leading up to March 2026, according to industry data. While more SUVs on the road does not necessarily mean more aggressive driving, the vehicles' size, height and presence can change the dynamics of a confrontation.

"For some drivers it is an expression of strength and domination," former police officer Yashovardhan Azad told DW.

"One drives with impunity to make an impression on smaller vehicles," said Azad.

He called for tougher policing using new technology, rigorous punishment and a nationwide programme to promote safer driving.

"Hitting a smaller vehicle intentionally is not rash driving. It is a measure of criminal intent," he said.

'SUV drivers have a beast in their hands'

Road safety expert Prince Singhal, founder of the Community Against Drunken Driving, sees both vehicles and drivers as parts of the problem.

"The issue of terror behind SUVs is not just a traffic challenge but also a behavioral issue," Singhal told DW.

"The SUV drivers have a beast in their hands and it's their mindset which decides the outcome."

Singhal notes that SUVs are a practical choice for bad roads and long journeys, but also points to issues in their design.

"High bonnets and elevated bumper heights increased the risk of fatal head and chest injuries for pedestrians, children, and cyclists and all other road users compared to traditional lower cars," added Singhal.

With an SUV at hand, drivers often experience "a psychological sense of invincibility," which can lead to hostile behavior, road bullying and rule violations, he said.

Are drivers taking traffic too personally?

Psychiatrist Ravi Prakash, who studies traffic behavior at Veditha Mind Care Clinic in Bengaluru, agrees that the driver "feels both powerful and protected inside a large, sturdy vehicle."

He also warned that there are other mechanisms at play.

"There is a psychological phenomenon called 'personalization,' where people interpret an ordinary act by a stranger as something personally directed at them," he told DW.

Someone cutting across a lane may be in a hurry. But the other driver may see it as an attempt to assert superiority. A perceived insult can then threaten a person's identity and trigger a spike of anger.

"Usually, hitting the other person is not the goal initially," Prakash said.

The driver first tries to assert superiority through speeding, honking, gestures or shouting. When that fails, a desire to punish can emerge, what Prakash calls an "illusion of retributive justice."

'Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture'

Sociologist Dipankar Gupta says road rage happens "because traffic rules are not strictly enforced," with the problem in no way limited to SUV drivers.

"Even motorcyclists get into road rage," he told DW.

"It's like a child who is not disciplined and throws a tantrum," Gupta said of the wider breakdown in road discipline. When rules are routinely ignored and people do not want to face the consequences, he added, it becomes similar to "a punch up" in school.

With cameras everywhere, however, such behavior has become harder to ignore.

"The anger is not new. What has changed is that everyone has a camera now, whether it is a dashcam, a helmet camera or a mobile phone," Deepanshu Gupta, cofounder of CrashFree India, a road safety nonprofit, told DW.

He warns that recording an incident is not the same as preventing it.

"Every driver knows that the odds of facing any real consequence are very low," he said.

"Anything that you tolerate becomes a culture. Aggressive driving is normalized here, but culture responds to enforcement," Deepanshu Gupta said.

He also noted that road rage is not a specifically defined offense in India, leaving police to choose between rash driving and far more serious charges such as attempted murder. "There is very little in between," he said.

In such conditions, responsibility rests on the drivers, particularly when a large vehicle is in a confrontation with a more vulnerable road user.

"The bigger the vehicle you bring onto the road, the greater your duty of care has to be," he said.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Russia: Putin party retains majority in controlled parliamentary vote
entries.summary: Vladimir Putin's United Russia won just under 58% of the vote, the electoral commission said. Meanwhile, Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov won nearly 100% of the vote in elections in the Russian republic of Chechnya.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia: Putin party retains majority in parliamentary vote

September 21, 2026

Vladimir Putin's United Russia won just under 58% of the vote, the electoral commission said. Meanwhile, Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov won nearly 100% of the vote in elections in the Russian republic of Chechnya.

Russia's electoral commission on Monday said that the ruling United Russia party has won the parliamentary election.

It's the first parliamentary poll since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and President Vladimir Putin has cast it as a referendum of support for what is termed in Russia, the "special military operation."

Parties that support Putin and the Kremlin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition was barred from taking part.

The polls took place amid rising prices, a crackdown on political opponents and the internet, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections.

What do we know about the Russian election results?

The Central Election Commission said that with 95% of ballots counted, the party of Russian President Vladimir Putin won 57.83% of the vote.

Commission chair Ella Pamfilova said that according to the preliminary results, United Russia would get 355 seats in the 450-seat Duma, giving the party around 20 more seats than it currently holds and marking the strongest result in its history.

The parliamentary vote was also the first to include residents of four regions in Ukraine — those being Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia —  that were occupied and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year.

Voting was also held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal.

Chechen ally receives nearly 100% of vote

Russia's electoral commission also announced that close Putin ally, Ramzan ​Kadyrov, has been re-elected to a fifth term as leader of Chechnya, a Russian republic in the North Caucasus region.

Electoral officials said he achieved 99.85% of the vote, a slight improvement from the 99.73% garnered in 2021.

International observers have previously severely criticised electoral processes in the small region.

Kadyrov's government has been accused of widespread rights violations by human rights organizations, including targeting journalists and homosexuals, something he denies.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

Skip next section Mercedes-Benz considers plant shutdowns in Germany if cost cuts fail

Mercedes-Benz considers plant shutdowns in Germany if cost cuts fail

German carmaker Mercedes-Benz could close two of its factories if it fails to reduce operating costs, the company's Head of Production, Michael Schiebe, warned during an employee meeting on Monday. 

"Our clear goal is to maintain all of our production sites in Germany," Schiebe said. "To achieve this, we must agree on measures that are acceptable to everyone in order to reduce costs in Germany. If we fail to do so, we will have to close a body shop and a German powertrain plant." 

The employee meeting took place in Sindelfingen, a city near Stuttgart, where thousands of workers took to the streets on Monday to protest job cuts and cost-reduction measures in the automotive industry. 

According to Schiebe, the facilities at risk are a body shop plant, where vehicles are assembled, and a powertrain plant, where automotive components are manufactured.

In Germany, Mercedes-Benz's body shop plants are located in Sindelfingen, Rastatt, and Bremen. Its powertrain plants are based in Untertürkheim, Affalterbach, Berlin, Hamburg, Kamenz, Kölleda, and Arnstadt.

Protests across Germany

IG Metall, the country's largest industrial union, said that around 175,000 employees took part in rallies on Monday at 280 locations, including key automotive hubs such as Stuttgart, Wolfsburg, Ingolstadt, and Munich. 

Mercedes-Benz has stepped up its cost-cutting efforts and announced a "productivity campaign for Germany."

With this move, the automaker has sparked a broader public debate about labor costs. The company's management board published an open letter to employees proposing longer working hours without additional pay.

Skip next section Oktoberfest debuts first event for queer women

Oktoberfest debuts first event for queer women

The first official party for queer women at Munich's Oktoberfest took place on Monday.

It is the first time in the history of the Bavarian festival that an event exclusively for lesbian women has been held. "There have been established queer events for decades, but so far lesbian women have hardly had a visible role as a community of their own," said co-organizer Sina Scherer, who also runs a series of events for Munich's queer community. 

"At some point, we said, 'We're not going to wait for someone to create a space for us. We'll create it ourselves," she added.

Although the first Sunday of the festival has long been celebrated by Germany's gay community, queer women had never before had their own official event at Oktoberfest. Scherer said many venues for lesbians had shut in Munich in recent years and warned that visibility remains a challenge for the community during Oktoberfest, the world-famous beer festival. 

Revelers gathered in one of the iconic "Festzelte," the large tents that accommodate thousands of people each year during the festival, under the slogan "Beer, Breasts, Pretzels." Attendees wore traditional dirndls as the rainbow flag flew above the stage. 

The party followed the traditional "Gay Sunday" celebration and welcomed members of the FLINTA community, a German acronym referring to women, lesbians, intersex, non-binary, trans, and agender people. Co-organizer Silke Völlig said about 700 people registered to attend the celebration.

Oktoberfest is held every year in Munich, the capital of the German state of Bavaria. It is the largest beer festival in the world and runs until October 4 this year. The event kicked off on Sunday.

More than six million visitors are expected to attend Oktoberfest, enjoy beer, amusement rides, traditional Bavarian food and live music. 

Skip next section Berlin says fuel price discount to take effect on October 1

Berlin says fuel price discount to take effect on October 1

The German government plans to approve a planned discount on gasoline on Monday and introduce it at the start of October, according to a Finance Ministry spokesperson.

The spokesperson said a draft bill on the discount had been finalized at the weekend and would likely be passed by both houses of parliament later this week.

The German government on Friday announced that it will cut taxes on gas and diesel by 17 cents ($0.20) per liter, days after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised relief for consumers and businesses hit by soaring fuel prices.

 The announcement comes after Merz's party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), suffered a heavy defeat in regional elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

German economy faces setback

Germany has endured an extended period of economic weakness since late 2022.

Europe's largest economy stagnated during the first half of 2026, with gross domestic product increasing by 0.4% in the first quarter and 0.3%, in the second.

Germany’s central bank said on Monday that the economy has experienced a "temporary loss of momentum" due to low water levels on the Rhine river and high energy prices. But Bundesbank expects growth to pick up back up toward the end of the year.

Skip next section Automotive workers protest nationwide as industry suffers crisis

Automotive workers protest nationwide as industry suffers crisis

Protesters from Germany's automotive industry have called for action from the government and company managements to save their jobs and factories as the country's car production sector faces a growing crisis.

Tens of thousands of people are expected to take part in rallies, which, according to the IG Metall union — Europe and Germany's largest — will take place at more than 280 sites.

Car industry being driven 'into a brick wall'

Speaking at carmaker Volkswagen's Wolfsburg factory, IG Metall's chairwoman, Christiane Benner, who is also a member of  VW's supervisory board, said: "Things have really hit the fan."

"Companies like VW, BMW, Audi, Bosch, Mercedes and Porsche were synonymous with fantastic cars and high quality," she said.

"Now, management is driving the industry at full throttle into a brick wall."

Benner called on the government to bring down energy costs, give financial help to suppliers to help them adjust to new challenges and use "Made in EU" rules to bolster domestic production.

Massive job cuts underway

Many observers put the blame for the current crisis on companies having started too late with the shift to electric vehicles, while others say China's government support for its own producers has led to an unequal playing field in the sector.

US tariffs have also done their bit to damage what is one of Germany's key industries, while domestic demand has weakened.

VW itself plans to cut 100,000 jobs by the end of the decade in what would be the biggest ever restructuring in global automotive history, while Mercedes-Benz and BMW are also reducing their workforces.

Skip next section German car exports down in first seven months of 2026 — Destatis

German car exports down in first seven months of 2026 — Destatis

In 2026, German exports of passenger cars dropped by 4% up to the end of July in comparison with the same period last year, new figures by the Federal Statistical Office showed on Monday.

It exported altogether some 2 million cars at a worth of €73.5 billion ($84.4 billion), 8.9% less than a year ago, with almost a third going to the UK, the US and Italy.

Cars with electric and combustion engines both saw an export drop of 2.9%, while the export of those with hybrid motors fell by 8.2%.

Imports of new passenger cars rose by 16% to some 1.3 million vehicles.

China takes first place for car imports

Chinese vehicles climbed to first place among car imports to Germany at 175,000 vehicles.

That made up 13.8% of all car imports and represents a rise of 120.9% compared with the January-July period in 2025.

It thus pushed the former import leaders Czech Republic and Spain to second and third place respectively.

The rise in Chinese imports was largely driven by hybrid vehicles (+36%) and purely electric vehicles (+66%), while imports of Chinese cars with combustion engines went down 9%.

Skip next section Elections latest: Merz defiant after state poll drubbings

Elections latest: Merz defiant after state poll drubbings

Friedrich Merz's position as chancellor is looking increasingly fragile after his Christian Democrats (CDU) failed to make it into the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in weekend elections.

And that result came on the heels of the election in Saxony-Anhalt around two weeks ago, in which the CDU also put in a poor showing amid big gains by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

That, combined with his already very low approval ratings, means Merz is currently under huge pressure.

DW looks at his predicament and the broader fallout from the recent polls in this dedicated blog: Germany: Friedrich Merz fights for survival after election defeats

Skip next section Germany brings in bumper cherry harvest

Germany brings in bumper cherry harvest

German orchard growers have harvested some 48,500 metric tons (53,462 US tons) of sweet and sour cherries this summer — 7.8% above the average for the past 10 years — new statistics show.

According to the German Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), some 80.2% of the harvest (38,900 tons) was sweet cherries, and 19.8% (9,600) was of the sour variety.

Pear growers also have reason to be content, with preliminary estimates putting the harvest of that fruit at 7.7% higher than the average over the past 10 years, though 3.3% down on last year.

The good fruit harvest comes despite Germany's grain production suffering greatly under the hot conditions during the summer.

Skip next section Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.

Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.

Both of them deny the charges made against them.

What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?

The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.

Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz,  had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.

The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.

But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.

The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.

Jail sentences possible

The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.

If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn wishes all its readers guten Tag at the start of a new week.

Among the big topics of the day in Germany is the start of a trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer in connection with a failed car toll scheme that cost the government hundreds of millions of euros some seven years ago.

He stands accused of making false statements before a parliamentary committee investigating the issue.

In more positive news, cherry (and pear) farmers have something to smile about this year: They have had their best harvest in years owing to some mild spring weather.

And we will also, of course, be looking at the fallout from recent state elections that have brought bad news for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

entries.title: Pakistan says strikes in Afghanistan killed '28 terrorists'
entries.summary: The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were struck overnight. Pakistan said 28 militants were killed, Afghanistan said three civilians died. This follows soon after an attack on police in Kohat, Pakistan.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan says strikes in Afghanistan killed '28 terrorists'

September 21, 2026

The Afghan border provinces of Kunar and Paktika were struck overnight. Pakistan said 28 militants were killed, Afghanistan said three civilians died. This follows soon after an attack on police in Kohat, Pakistan.

Pakistan conducted airstrikes on northeastern Afghanistan on Monday on what Pakistan's Ministry of Information described as suicide bomber training facilities. 

It was the first Pakistani strike of its kind on Afghan territory since June, and followed soon after an attack targeting Pakistani police across the border in Kohat. 

The uneasy neighbors reported seemingly conflicting casualty tolls.

What were the conflicting accounts on the strikes?

Pakistan's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting claimed online that the attacks had targeted terrorist training sites in Afghanistan with "precision and accuracy."

"Three targets were destroyed with precision including a Suicide Bombers training markaz [station], killing 28 terrorists alongside multiple suicide bombers. Large quantities of weapons and ammunition ... were also destroyed," the Ministry said.

The Taliban government in Kabul, meanwhile, claimed that three people were killed as it accused Pakistan of bombarding "civilian homes." 

Afghanistan's deputy government spokesperson Hamdullah Fitrat said that the strikes took place in the Kunar and Paktika provinces.

Fitrat wrote on X that one strike hit at around 3:00 am Monday (2230 UTC, Sunday) in Kunar's Nurgal district and "completely destroyed" a house, adding that three people were killed and four other members of the family were wounded.

He said that two locations were also hit in the Paktika province, claiming that a shop and an unoccupied house were destroyed.

Neither side's assertions on the details of and casualties from the strikes could be immediately verified. 

Strikes follow last week's militant attack in Pakistan

The reported strikes come after a suicide bombing and a 20-hour gun battle between militants and police on Friday, which took place at a district police headquarters compound in the Pakistani city of Kohat, situated near the Afghan border.

At least 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed in the attack.

Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a local militant group linked to the jihadist group Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), claimed responsibility for the attack.

The Afghanistan-Pakistan conflict

Relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan have been tense since the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

The latest strikes threaten to shatter three months of relative calm after former South Asian allies engaged in their worst clashes in years in February.

Pakistan declared that month that it was in an "open war” with Afghanistan, following a rise in militant attacks on civilians and security forces inside Pakistan.

Afghanistan launched retaliatory strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes inside Afghan territory and the cross-border fighting has since claimed the lives of hundreds of people.

Pakistan last mounted deadly airstrikes in Afghanistan in June.

Islamabad accuses Afghanistan of sheltering militant groups which launch attacks inside Pakistan's territory.

Main among these is the TTP, often referred to as the Pakistani Taliban and Baloch separatist groups from the border areas.

The Taliban has dismissed ​the allegations, saying that militancy in Pakistan is an internal problem.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

entries.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
entries.summary: German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on workers' rights.
entries.content:
September 21, 2026

German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on workers' rights.

Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.  

Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.

Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.

Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.

Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.

"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."

Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.

Labor costs too high in Germany?

Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.

Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a reportpublished by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.

To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.

The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.

It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."

Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.

Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.

The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.

IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.

Can longer working hours save jobs?

The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.

The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.

"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.

Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.

On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.

"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.

How can Germany's auto industry recover?

Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.

"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.

He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.

"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.

At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.

Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.

"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.

And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.

"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."

Edited by: Tim Rooks
